title: RoPE, explained: turn position into an angle, and attention only sees relative distance
summary: The RoFormer paper introduces RoPE: instead of adding a position vector to each token, it rotates the query and key by an angle based on position, so the dot product depends only on position difference. We work through the 2D rotation math, the speed table, and long-range decay, then look at which experimental claims in the paper hold up and which need caveats.
ai_summary: RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding (Jianlin Su et al., Zhuiyi Technology, 2021) introduced RoPE: it treats each pair of dimensions of the query and key as a plane and rotates them by an angle determined by the token's position, so the dot product depends only on the relative distance between the two tokens. The paper derives this solution in the 2D case, gives a family of rotation frequencies from fast to slow with base 10000 and an element-wise implementation, proves that an upper bound on the dot product decays with distance, and shows that RoPE is compatible with linear attention. Experiments include WMT14 English-German translation, BERT-style pretraining, GLUE, Performer, and Chinese long-text matching; in the GLUE section, the BERT baseline is taken from the original paper's test set and is not fully comparable with this paper's validation-set results.
brief: Problem: attention doesn't know word order; existing position encodings are all additive, and relative position encodings also require changing the expanded attention score.
Method: rotate queries and keys by position, with a different speed for each dimension pair; only relative position remains in the dot product.
Results: pretraining converges faster; Chinese long-text models can read 1024 positions and do better; it works directly with linear attention.
Limitations: experiments are small; GLUE is three wins and three losses and the baselines aren't measured on the same yardstick; the authors themselves can't explain why convergence is faster.

paper.title: RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding
paper.authors: Jianlin Su, Yu Lu, Shengfeng Pan, Ahmed Murtadha, Bo Wen, Yunfeng Liu

cover.headline: A close read of the RoPE paper
cover.highlight: Position is the angle of rotation

nodes.label: The dot product keeps only n − m

sections.h: The short version: what this paper actually does

blocks.p: In April 2021, six authors led by Jianlin Su at Shenzhen-based Zhuiyi Technology posted this paper on arXiv. It introduced rotary position embedding (RoPE), which later became one of the most common ways for open-source large language models to tell the model which position each token occupies; LLaMA, which we've covered before, uses it.

The problem comes from the Transformer itself: attention only sees which tokens resemble which, so it has no built-in sense of word order, and position information must be supplied separately. Previous approaches were almost all additive: give each position a vector and add it to the token vector (absolute position), or add a distance-dependent term to the attention score (relative position).

RoPE changes this to multiplication, and a special kind of multiplication: rotation. Treat each pair of dimensions in the query and key as an arrow on a plane, and rotate the arrow for the m-th token by m times a fixed angle. The dot product of two arrows depends only on the angle between them, so the attention score between the m-th and n-th tokens naturally depends only on the distance n − m: absolute positions are encoded, but the result is relative.

The paper also proves RoPE has two good properties: the farther apart two tokens are, the smaller an upper bound on the dot product becomes (long-range decay); and it can be used directly with linear attention, which earlier relative position encodings could not. The experiments are modest: translation, BERT-style pretraining, GLUE fine-tuning, Performer, and Chinese long-text matching.

callout.title: One-sentence version
callout.text: Instead of adding a position vector to token vectors, rotate the query and key by an angle based on their position. Once the two rotated vectors are dotted, only their position difference remains, so attention naturally sees only relative distance.

callout.title: Three small concepts you need for this read
callout.text: If you don't know them, these three are enough:
list: **Dot product**: multiply the corresponding entries of two vectors and add them up. In a 2D plane, that equals the product of the two arrow lengths times the cosine of the angle between them: the more aligned their directions, the larger the value.
**Query (q) and key (k) in attention**: each token computes a q and a k; the dot product of token m's q and token n's k determines how much m attends to n. See the Transformer close read for details.
**Rotation**: turn an arrow in a plane around the origin by some angle; its length stays the same, and only its direction changes.

sections.h: Problem: how does a Transformer know word order?

blocks.p: Give an attention layer with no position information the phrases "dog bites man" and "man bites dog," and it sees the same bag of words and produces the same result. That is why every Transformer needs extra position encoding. The paper divides existing approaches into two kinds:

list: **Absolute position encoding**: give the i-th position a vector p_{i} and add it to the token vector before computing q, k, and v. The original Transformer generates p_{i} with sine and cosine functions; BERT and GPT treat it as trainable parameters. The drawback is that the model learns "position 37," while language usually cares more about "the third word before this one"; trainable versions also only learn up to a maximum length L.

**Relative position encoding**: split the attention score q_{m}^{⊺} k_{n} into four terms and replace the position-dependent terms with something that looks only at the distance m − n. Transformer-XL, DeBERTa, and T5 belong to this family: T5 simply adds a learnable bias for each distance. The drawback is that it modifies the expanded attention score, so it is tied to the attention computation formula.

blocks.p: The paper points out that these methods all rest on the idea of adding position into the representation. It asks the reverse question: can we directly find functions that encode position into q and k so that their dot product automatically depends only on relative position? In a formula:

parts.desc: Functions that combine the m-th token's vector x_{m} and its position m into the query and key; those are what we need to solve for.
The dot product, i.e., the core of the attention score.
A function that depends only on the token vectors and the position difference m − n; the absolute positions m and n may not appear separately.

formula.note: Section 3.4.1 of the paper solves this equation in the 2D case: length must not change with position, and angle must grow uniformly with position. The answer is rotation.

plain.title: Only the difference in steps matters
plain.text: Two people stand on a staircase: one pair is on steps 2 and 5, another pair on steps 9 and 12. They stand at different heights, but both are 3 steps apart. That is the attention score the paper wants: it sees only how far apart two tokens are, not where in the sentence they sit.

sections.h: Core idea: position is the angle you rotate by

blocks.p: Start with the simplest 2D case. q and k are arrows on a plane. Let the query at position m rotate by mθ and the key at position n rotate by nθ, where θ is a fixed angle chosen in advance:

parts.desc: As in standard attention, first project the token vector into a query.
The 2D rotation matrix: rotates an arrow counterclockwise by α while keeping its length unchanged.
Rotating both sides once is equivalent to rotating only k by the difference between their angles. The absolute positions m and n disappear, leaving only n − m.

formula.note: Complex form is cleaner: q_{m} = q · e^{imθ}, k_{n} = k · e^{inθ}, and the dot product is the real part of q · k^{*} · e^{i(m−n)θ}. That is equation (12) in the paper.

plain.title: Each side rotates; the angle only depends on how many ticks apart
plain.text: Think of the query and key as two hands on a clock face: the query at position m rotates m ticks, and the key at position n rotates n ticks. On the left, m = 2 and n = 3; on the right, m = 10 and n = 11. The two hands point in different directions, but the angle between them is one tick (30°) in both cases. Dot product depends only on that angle, so it only knows n − m.

fig.title: Hand calculation: same distance, same attention score
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: 2D case with q = k = (1, 0) and each position rotating by θ = 30°. Dot product = cos((n − m) × 30°), computed here from equation (12) of the paper.
fig.note: The second and third rows have completely different positions but the same distance, so their dot products are equal. But the last row exposes the problem: with a single angle, distance 12 rotates all the way back to the origin and cannot be distinguished from distance 0. That's why real RoPE needs many different angles.

callout.title: Like a wall clock
callout.text: A clock with only a second hand returns to the same spot after one minute, so it can't tell 1 second from 61 seconds. Add the minute hand and the hour hand, and the three hands together can distinguish a long span of time. RoPE splits the vector into many pairs and gives each pair a different speed: fast pairs resolve nearby distances, slow pairs resolve faraway distances.

sections.h: Generalizing to high dimensions: many dimension pairs, many speeds

blocks.p: For a d-dimensional vector (d even), split it into d/2 adjacent pairs of dimensions. Each pair rotates in its own plane, and the i-th pair's speed is θ_{i}:

parts.desc: A block-diagonal matrix: place d/2 2×2 rotation blocks along the diagonal; the i-th block rotates by mθ_{i}.
The angle, in radians, that the i-th dimension pair rotates by per position. The first pair rotates 1 radian; later pairs are slower, and the slowest approaches 1/10000.
The base is borrowed from the original Transformer's sinusoidal position encoding.

formula.note: These rotation matrices are orthogonal, so they do not change vector length, which the paper says keeps position encoding stable. Note: RoPE rotates only q and k, not v; and it is applied in the attention of every layer, not just added once at the input.

plain.title: At the same moment, fast hands and slow hands each point somewhere
plain.text: Each dimension pair is a clock with a different speed: θ₁ is the fastest, θ₄ is the slowest. For the same position (the 7th token), the four clocks point in different directions. Fast clocks resolve nearby distances, slow clocks resolve faraway distances, and together they can tell a long range of positions apart.

fig.title: From fast to slow: how many positions each pair takes to make one full turn
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: d = 128, using θ_{i} from equation (15) of the paper; "one full turn" = 2π / θ_{i}, computed here.
fig.note: As with a clock: the fast dimension pairs are sensitive to nearby position differences, and the slow pairs change gradually, which lets them resolve very long distances. The last column is a rough explanatory shorthand, not a conclusion from the paper.

blocks.p: In practice, you do not need to multiply by a large matrix that is mostly 0. Section 3.4.2 gives an element-wise form: two element-wise multiplications plus one addition are enough.

parts.desc: Swap the two numbers in each pair and negate the first: that is exactly a 90° rotation of that pair.
Depend only on position m, so they can be precomputed and reused.

plain.title: A 90° rotation is "swap and negate"
plain.text: Rotating a coordinate pair (x, y) by 90° gives (−y, x). So rotating by any angle = original coordinates × cos + the 90°-rotated coordinates × sin. Do this element-wise over the whole vector — multiply twice and add once — and you never need an actual large matrix multiplication.

sections.h: Three properties: relative position, long-range decay, and linear attention

blocks.p: **1. Relative position built in.** The previous section showed it: q and k each rotate by their own absolute position, and only the position difference remains in the dot product. Unlike earlier relative position encodings, there is no need to change the attention score formula — just rotate q and k before computing the dot product.

**2. Long-range decay.** Section 3.4.3 proves that as distance grows, an upper bound on the q-k dot product shrinks. The intuition: for position difference r, the i-th dimension pair's contribution is multiplied by a unit arrow rotated by rθ_{i}. When r = 0, all arrows point the same way; as r grows, arrows at different speeds point in increasingly scattered directions and cancel out more when summed. The paper plots this decay with one quantity (Figure 2); we recomputed it from the paper's definition:

fig.title: Greater distance, smaller upper bound
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: d = 128, using the quantity (1 / (d/2)) · Σ|S_{j}| from Section 3.4.3, where S_{j} is the sum of the first j unit arrows; numbers computed here.
fig.note: This is an upper bound, not the attention score itself: distant tokens can still receive a high score, but the ceiling is lower. The paper says this matches the intuition that tokens far apart usually have weaker relationships.

plain.title: A crowd of arrows: aligned is long, scattered is short
plain.text: At position difference 0, each dimension pair contributes an arrow in the same direction; placed end to end, they form one long line. Once the distance grows, each pair rotates by a different angle, so the arrows point every which way; laid end to end, they do not travel far from the start. That is how the upper bound on the dot product shrinks with distance.

blocks.p: **3. Works with linear attention.** Standard attention computes a score for every token pair, so cost grows quadratically with sequence length. Linear attention (such as Performer) first transforms q and k using a non-negative function, then uses the associativity of matrix multiplication to reduce cost to linear in length. Earlier relative position encodings modify each pairwise score, so this shortcut is not available to them. RoPE only rotates the transformed q and k individually — no pairwise matching is needed — so it applies directly.

The tradeoff is that, to avoid dividing by zero, the paper keeps the denominator unrotated, while the numerator may contain negative terms, so the weight for each value is no longer strictly a probability that sums to 1. The paper acknowledges this and says it "can still model the importance of values."

callout.title: "RoPE is just a better position vector added to token vectors"
callout.text: No. RoPE has no position vector to add: it applies a position-dependent rotation to q and k in every attention layer, while the token vectors themselves and v carry no position. That is its fundamental difference from the original Transformer, BERT, and GPT position encodings: addition becomes multiplication.

sections.h: Experiments: small in scale, so separate the conclusions

blocks.p: All of the paper's experiments ran on two cloud servers, each with 4 V100 GPUs — far smaller than later large-model work. The main results:

list: **Machine translation**: on WMT 2014 English-to-German (about 4.5M sentence pairs), replacing the original Transformer-base position encoding with RoPE raises BLEU from 27.3 to 27.5. The paper reports only this one number and no run-to-run variance.
**BERT-style pretraining**: with BERT's position encoding replaced by RoPE, batch size 64, max length 512, and 100k training steps, the masked language model loss drops faster (Figure 3 left).
**Performer**: on Enwik8, adding RoPE to a 12-layer linear attention model lowers the loss faster and further under the same step count (Figure 3 right).

blocks.p: **GLUE fine-tuning** is the section to read carefully. The paper says RoFormer "significantly surpasses" BERT on three of six tasks:

fig.title: RoFormer vs. BERT: three wins, three losses, and not the same yardstick
fig.subtitle: From Table 2 of the paper. The BERT row exactly matches the GLUE test-set scores in Table 1 of the original BERT paper; the RoFormer row, according to the paper, is the best average validation-set score.
fig.note: RoFormer is higher on MRPC, STS-B, and QQP, and lower on SST-2, QNLI, and MNLI. The 15-point gap on QQP is the most eye-catching, but with one side from a test set and the other from a validation set, that gap cannot be credited to RoPE.

blocks.p: **Chinese long text** is the result the paper most wants to establish. The authors replaced WoBERT's absolute position encoding with RoPE, trained on about 34GB of Chinese text in six stages with different maximum lengths (128 to 1536), then evaluated on CAIL2019-SCM, a legal case matching dataset of 8,964 triples, with most documents exceeding 512 characters:

fig.title: Long text: RoFormer can read 1024 positions
fig.subtitle: From Table 5 of the paper. Accuracy (%), higher is better. The number after each model name is the maximum input length.
fig.note: When all three are cut to 512, they nearly tie; RoFormer's advantage comes from reading longer inputs. Note that BERT and WoBERT use absolute position encodings learned only up to 512, so they can't be directly compared with the 1024-length version.

blocks.p: The paper ends by admitting two limitations: it can't explain why RoPE converges faster than other position encodings, and it can't explain why it does better on long text, since the long-range decay property is shared by other position encodings.

sections.h: A few details worth a closer look

list: **Inconsistent θ subscript.** Equation (15) writes θ_{i} = 10000^{−2(i−1)/d} with i starting at 1; Sections 3.3 and 3.4.3 write θ_{i} = 10000^{−2i/d}. The two differ by one index. It doesn't change the idea, but pick one convention before implementing.

**The GLUE comparison isn't the same yardstick.** The six BERT numbers in Table 2 are exactly the same as the GLUE test-set scores in the original BERT paper, while this paper says it reports validation-set results. It doesn't say where the BERT row comes from, and it doesn't mention that RoFormer scores lower on the other three tasks.

**The “1.5% improvement” doesn't match the table.** Section 4.5.4 says RoFormer-1024 is an absolute 1.5% improvement over WoBERT, but in Table 5 the test-set gap is 1.69 (69.79 vs. 68.10) and the validation-set gap is 2.00 (66.07 vs. 64.07). The only place with exactly a 1.5-point gap is RoFormer-1024 against its own 512 version (69.79 vs. 68.29). And a 1024-vs-512 comparison already includes the advantage of reading longer input.

**Sign of the position difference.** Equation (11) writes g(x_{m}, x_{n}, m − n), while equation (21) in the derivation writes n − m. They're just different conventions, but a single paper should stay consistent.
**A subscript typo.** Equation (32) writes q = f_{q}(x_{m}, 0) = W_{q} x_{n}; the right-hand side should be x_{m}.
**Typo in the Table 2 caption.** GLUE is written as “GLEU.”

sections.h: Afterward: the most widely used position encoding in open-source LLMs

list: **LLaMA and later open-source models.** The LLaMA paper states that it removes absolute position encoding and adds RoPE in every layer of the network. Many open-source models since have followed.

**Stretching context.** RoPE's rotation speeds are determined by the base 10000. Later work found that by “squeezing” positions into the trained range, or by adjusting the speed of different dimensions, the model's readable length could be expanded several times over. This became a common technique for long-context models.

**A small implementation difference.** The paper pairs adjacent dimensions; many popular implementations instead pair each dimension in the first half with the corresponding dimension in the second half. This merely reorders the dimensions and is mathematically equivalent, but you have to match it when reusing someone else's weights.

**Connection to this line of work.** T5 uses relative position in the form of one learnable bias per distance. RoPE gets the same relativity through rotation, without changing the attention score formula.

blocks.p: Next, we return to the attention computation itself: **FlashAttention**. It doesn't change the result attention computes; it rearranges the order in which attention reads and writes memory so that long-sequence attention is both faster and more memory-efficient.

sections.h: Test yourself: did you really get it?

quiz.q: How does RoPE make attention scores depend only on relative position?
options: Learn a bias for each distance and add it to the score
Rotate q by mθ at position m and k by nθ at position n; the two rotations cancel in the dot product into a single rotation that depends only on n − m
Add a position vector to the token vector
Mask out tokens that are too far apart
quiz.why: Rotation doesn't change length, and the dot product of two rotated vectors depends only on the difference between their angles. So the absolute positions m and n cancel out, leaving only n − m.

quiz.q: Why does RoPE use different rotation speeds for different dimension pairs?
options: With only one speed, after a full turn the vector returns to the start, so near and far become indistinguishable. Mixing fast and slow speeds is what lets it resolve both nearby and distant positions.
To make the vector length smaller
To be compatible with BERT's weights
quiz.why: Like a clock with only a second hand can't tell 1 second from 61 seconds: fast dimension pairs resolve nearby position differences, and slow pairs resolve distant ones.

quiz.q: In Table 2, RoFormer scores 86.4 to BERT's 71.2 on QQP. Why can't this be treated as a big win for RoPE?
options: Because QQP is not a GLUE task
Because the BERT row is from the original paper's test set and RoFormer is from the validation set, so they aren't measured on the same yardstick
Because QQP is only for long text
quiz.why: The BERT row matches the GLUE test-set results in the original BERT paper exactly, while this paper reports validation-set results. Scores on the same task can differ a lot between the two sets.

blocks.p: After this close read, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: Why does the Transformer need position encoding, and what are the drawbacks of absolute and relative position encodings?
What exactly is being rotated in RoPE, and why does the dot product end up with only relative position?
What does θ_{i} = 10000^{−2(i−1)/d} mean, and why do there need to be fast and slow speeds?
What does long-range decay mean, and why is it only an upper bound?
Why can RoPE be combined with linear attention while previous relative position encodings cannot?
Among the paper's experiments, which conclusions are reliable and which need to be discounted?
